$comment: The single source of truth for every status claim in this repository.
README.md, docs/QUESTIONS.md, docs/ROADMAP.md and the marketing site all
render from this file via `mix ash_enterprise.roadmap`, which CI checks.
A status can therefore be wrong in one place only by being wrong in all of
them -- which is the point. Legal statuses: shipped | partial | planned | open.
shipped -- built, covered by a named test, and running in a deployment we operate.
`proof` is the test's file and `test` its name, which CI finds in that
file; `built` is the commit that built what the test proves.
partial -- works, with a named limitation stated in the answer.
planned -- an ADR and a plan exist, no code.
open    -- named as a gap, no decision taken.

sections.title: Who are you, and what may you do?
What happened, and can you prove it?
Where does data come from, and where does it go?
How does it change, and keep running?

questions.question: How do people prove who they are?
questions.answer: Password sign-in through `ash_authentication`, with remember-me, email confirmation and password reset; sign-in through the deployment's OpenID Connect identity provider when the build configures one (q29, ADR 0071); and API keys for the API and MCP pipelines. Sign-in issues a token that is stored server-side and expires after 8 hours (set explicitly, not the library's 14 days), the session cookie expires with it, and changing a password logs the user out everywhere. Five failed password sign-ins for one address lock it for 15 minutes, counted atomically in Postgres whether or not the address exists. The API and MCP pipelines read either an ordinary user token or a hashed API key from the bearer header; a key must carry an expiry (90 days at most), can be revoked, and stops working when its owner is deactivated. The unused magic-link route and its confirmation hook are removed. Not built: SAML and WebAuthn. OIDC sign-in is built and tested but not yet running in a deployment we operate.
questions.test: a correct password signs the user in and issues a token

questions.question: How is "may this actor do this?" decided?
questions.answer: `(role, privilege, depth)` rows evaluated as a pure union of grants — authorization is data, not code. No deny rules, so order cannot matter.
questions.test: two narrow grants union rather than conflict

questions.question: Who owns a record?
questions.answer: Polymorphic user-or-team ownership inherited from the base resource. The Dataverse ownership type per entity is scraped from the corpus, never guessed.
questions.test: basic reaches a record owned by a team the actor is on, and not one owned by another team

questions.question: How does where you sit in the org chart change what you can see?
questions.answer: A business-unit tree with a materialized path, plus an optional manager/position hierarchy. Grant depth expands to a subtree once per request, never inside a policy check.
questions.test: deep reaches the business unit and everything beneath it

questions.question: Can one record be shared with someone the rules would not otherwise reach?
questions.answer: An `AccessGrant` row — Dataverse's `PrincipalObjectAccess` — adds rights to one record without widening any role.
questions.test: the pinned app shows less: the revoked rows are not sent, not just flagged

questions.question: Are some columns more sensitive than the rows that contain them?
questions.answer: Yes, for reads, on the base resource and keyed by grants (ADR 0073). A resource lists `secured_fields`; reading one takes a role granting the column's own `:read` privilege (`prvReadCredential.number`), written into the catalogue at every boot, at a depth that reaches the row. A row grant does not include it, the Administrator holds every column, and there is no deny rule. Without the grant the value reads as hidden, and a filter or search on it matches nothing. A finding that copies it (what the licence reader found on the credential's own detail and tour) is masked the same way, and a test fails any expression calculation or aggregate in the application that reads a secured column. The first secured column is a credential's licence number. `LinkedAccount` keeps its hand-written policy on `connection_id` beside it. Partial: a write to a secured column still follows the row's grant, a sort on one is not rewritten, and a copy kept in another record (the licence document's text, the reader's judgment rows, the run that read it) is read through that record's own grants.

questions.question: Is every change recorded, including who and from where?
questions.answer: `AshEvents` writes a central append-only log on every create, update and destroy of a resource on the platform base, by default — inherited from the base resource, not wired per resource, so a new table cannot quietly have no history. A resource opts out only with `audit?: false` in its own file; among those that do are the append-only logs (model calls, agent run journals, the business-event ledger), read-only lookups and sync cursors. Who is recorded: the event names the acting user, and its metadata names a system actor, an automation principal and the person it acted for, or an impersonator, under a correlation id shared by every write of one request. Not recorded: where the change came from. No network address, user agent or client is captured, so a change can be tied to the request that made it but not to the place it was made from.
questions.test: assigning a role records the grantor, the grantee and the request's correlation id

questions.question: Can you follow one request across the whole system at 3am?
questions.answer: One correlation id per request, stamped into audit metadata and OTel spans, and carried across process boundaries explicitly.
questions.test: with_correlation/2 joins work done in another scope

questions.question: Are illegal state transitions impossible, or merely discouraged?
questions.answer: `ash_state_machine` generates one named action per legal transition from the canonical Dataverse lifecycle. There is no generic `:update` that can set a state.
questions.test: an illegal transition is rejected

questions.question: Can a deletion be undone?
questions.answer: A destroy archives the row instead of deleting it: `ash_archival` soft delete, inherited from the base resource, with an explicit `archival?: false` that a reviewer can grep for. A team can now be restored: `Team.restore` clears `archived_at` on a team archived within the restore window (30 days by default, `AshEnterprise.Platform.Validations.WithinRestoreWindow`), found through the `:archived` read. It is human-only and counted as changing authority, so no system actor, engine or automation principal reaches it; it needs write on teams; and the restore is audited with the person who did it. The refusals are tested: no write grant, a system actor, another tenant, outside the window, and a team never deleted. Partial because it is one resource: the other soft-deletable resources have no restore action, so undoing their deletion is still an operator's database operation.
questions.test: brings a deleted team back, and the log records who did it

questions.question: Can you rebuild state by replaying the log?
questions.answer: The `AshEvents` replay machinery is wired, and the clear step is now a configured list (`AshEnterprise.Audit.ClearRecordsForReplay`): it clears only the resources it names, and only where `allow?` is true, which dev and test set and production does not, so production still refuses. It also refuses before deleting anything when the log holds events of an audited resource the list does not name (replay re-runs every event), when events have moved to the archive (replay reads only the hot log), or when the list names the audit log or an unaudited resource. A test replays a log of business units created, nested and renamed, and gets back the same rows, and the replay records no new events. Partial because only that resource is proven: a full rebuild of every resource has not been run, and once retention has archived events the hot log alone cannot rebuild state.
questions.test: the listed resources, row for row

questions.question: How are tenants separated?
questions.answer: Attribute multitenancy on `organization_id`, inherited by every resource — never schema-per-tenant, and never per-department.
questions.test: creating with the resolved tenant sets the discriminator

questions.question: Does tenant isolation hold even when authorization is wrong?
questions.answer: Yes, and it is asserted as a separate property: the conformance suite checks isolation independently of every grant path.
questions.test: a global grant does not cross tenants

questions.question: Can you erase a person on request?
questions.answer: Partly, by crypto-shredding (ADR 0024's erasure half). Content that arrives through an external connection -- raw landings, canonical messages, conversations and calendar events, and the copies of that content in the audit log -- is sealed under that connection's erasure-scope key, and `shred_scope` destroys the key: rows, structural columns and the audit hash chain survive, the content reads as an explicit `shredded` marker. What is missing for a *person*: nothing yet lands under a `data_subject` scope, `Canonical.Person` names and emails are not sealed, core platform resources (users, organizations) are not covered, and soft delete is still the only delete. Backups and WAL keep the wrapped key until they age out.

questions.question: Where does the data physically live?
questions.answer: Partly. ADR 0042 declares zones: a jurisdiction, a classification ceiling and the residency restrictions a zone cannot satisfy. Data is admitted into a store only if its own tags are admissible there, and every unknown case (no zone, an untagged row, a malformed tag, a zone past its review date) is refused. The admission rule is built and used on the Gmail and Slack projection path. Nothing is declared by default, so a deployment that declares no zone fails closed; the rule is added per ingest action rather than inherited by every resource; and tenancy is still attribute-based in one database, so physical placement of the database itself is the deployment's.

questions.question: How does data get in from systems you do not own?
questions.answer: An Oban job runs a Meltano/Singer tap and lands raw rows in an operator-only landing resource sealed for erasure; host-declared projections promote them into ordinary platform resources, so ingested data acquires ownership, tenancy and audit at promotion. Provider APIs (Gmail, Calendar, Slack) land into the same resource through Nango. The schema-to-resource generator is not built.

questions.question: How do you integrate N SaaS systems without writing N×M integrations?
questions.answer: One contract per category rather than one per (your app × their API). Nango holds the provider edge — OAuth, token refresh, the proxy — and the sync logic stays here as Ash actions over Oban, so a policy gates which actor may trigger a sync and the ordinary audit log records it. Nango's free self-hosted edition gates syncs and webhooks, which is why the design is split that way rather than generated wholesale. Built for Google Calendar, Gmail and Slack (2026-10-12); webhooks are not.

questions.question: Can you trace a value back to the system it came from?
questions.answer: At the job and dataset level, yes. `ash_open_lineage` emits OpenLineage events from every platform write and every sync, and `AshEnterprise.Lineage` stores them as jobs, runs and job runs, drawn as a graph at `/app/lineage`. A run's id is the correlation id the audit log already carries, so the audit entries of a run and the run of an audit entry are each a lookup. Events carry names only, never an actor, a tenant or a value. Not built: tracing one value back to its source system. Neither Meltano nor Airbyte emits OpenLineage, so the graph has a hole exactly where external data enters, and that is stated rather than drawn over. Lineage rows are kept for 14 days.

questions.question: What data do you have, and who owns it?
questions.answer: A generated, read-only inventory of declared schema and ownership kind: `mix ash_enterprise.data_inventory` writes `docs/data-inventory.json` from the declarations every resource was compiled with, and CI fails when the file is stale. Each entry carries the domain, table, ownership kind, tenant-scoped or global, audit and archival switches, CDM provenance, API exposure, and which attributes are `sensitive?` or sealed. Classification is derived, never declared: a narrow name heuristic flags attributes that look personal, and one that is neither sensitive, sealed nor listed with a reason fails the check. It is a projection of the code, not a second source of truth, and it makes no claim of compatibility with any catalogue's schema. Not built: named data stewards (ownership here is a resource-level kind, which says who may be granted access, not who is accountable; accountable people are a deployment owner's input), a push to an external catalogue, and any attestation of what a running deployment holds.
questions.test: every platform resource appears with ownership, tenancy, audit, archival, api exposure, sensitive and sealed attributes

questions.question: How do people get reports out of it?
questions.answer: Superset over views already filtered by the same actor context, so the BI tool's row-level security is a formality rather than a duplicate authorization model. Metabase loses because its RLS is paywalled.

questions.question: The same customer arrived from three systems — which one is real?
questions.answer: In-Ash resolution is built. Source records land with temporal history; deterministic and fuzzy matching are banded by a DMN table; a steward queue takes person-gated verdicts; and a merge picks a winner per attribute under the tenant's survivorship policy, which can rank sources (`source_rank`), records the provenance of each choice with the source and statement it came from, repoints the source identities and can be unmerged, all under one correlation id. The golden record is an ordinary platform resource, so it inherits ownership, tenancy, audit and policy.
questions.test: source_rank works on a merge, and names the winning source

questions.question: How do you move onto this platform from a database you cannot stop?
questions.answer: `ash_strangler` maps a well-modelled resource onto the legacy schema through a closed grammar of typed combinators whose reverses are built rather than guessed, and moves it through four cutover phases without hand-written SQL. **Running here**: `legacy.users` is read through a compatibility view as an ordinary platform resource, a durable change ledger drained by an Oban worker (with a five-minute sweep as the recovery net) keeps that surface live, the same change is *projected* into a table this application owns, and a nightly reconcile compares the view with that table by checksum over key ranges, repairs what disagrees and reports counts and key ranges (`docs/runbooks/legacy-migration.md`). That is moving onto the platform while the source keeps running: read, project, reconcile. Still partial, and deliberately: this is not a cutover, and it is one entity on the same database instance. The legacy database remains the system of record, and the mapping is not invertible in documented places (`full_name` cannot be split back into first and last, five legacy states collapse onto two lifecycle statuses, `company_id` is unmapped), which is exactly what a true cutover would have to resolve.

questions.question: How do the processes people actually follow get modelled?
questions.answer: `ash_bpmn` compiles a BPMN document into an immutable versioned graph and executes it with a token interpreter over Postgres and Oban, with an embedded designer. Gateway conditions are FEEL, the DMN expression language -- the hand-written expression evaluator it replaced is deleted. **Running here**: the six resources sit on the platform base resource, so a process instance is an ordinary owned, tenant-scoped record and the engine's bypass is the first policy in the base's own set. A published baseline, four seeded requests covering every branch of the gateway, and two tenants on different versions of the same key.
questions.test: a low-risk request is granted without a human

questions.question: How does an action get a second person's approval before it takes effect?
questions.answer: A change dropped on any action: work item, materialized candidate list, maker-checker exclusion applied by subtraction at candidate resolution rather than as a `forbid_if`, delegation, and escalation timers that get cancelled. **A work item is a platform resource here** -- owned, tenant-scoped and audited -- so who may approve is the same union of grants as who may read, and both the manager and executive approval branches are reachable in the demo. The refusals are now asserted, not only the positive case: a member who is not a candidate, a member whose role reads every task, a candidate for another task and another tenant's candidate are each refused and the task stays open.
questions.test: a member of the same tenant who is not a candidate cannot decide the task

questions.question: How do API contracts change without breaking the callers you cannot see?
questions.answer: Version deltas declared as data on the resource — one schema, N presentation contracts, no second table or view — with `render`/`parse` invertibility checked at compile time and sunset proposed from real traffic.

questions.question: How do you ship a change to some users first?
questions.answer: Through tenant feature flags (ADR 0072). A build declares its flags; each tenant decides who sees one with an audited, tenant-scoped row: off, on for everyone in the tenant, or targeted at named people, the members of named teams, the subtree of named business units, and a percentage of people by a bucket that is stable per person and key. The rows are resolved once per request (and before every LiveView event) into the person's `ActorContext`, so checking a flag is a set lookup that never queries, and a change reaches a person at their next request or event. An undeclared key is off; `FLAGS_OFF` kills a key in every tenant without touching a row. Flipping a flag is a person's act, needs a grant, and is in the audit log. Policies are not a substitute and never read a flag: they answer *may you*, not *is this on*, and conflating them produces a `beta_user` role you then have to revoke from everyone. Not provided: environments, percentage-of-time, scheduled flips and a management screen (flags are managed through the code interface and `mix ash_enterprise.flags`). Not yet running in a deployment we operate.
questions.test: a flag targeted at a team is on for its members and off for everyone else

questions.question: How does the schema itself evolve without drifting from the model?
questions.answer: Migrations are derived as a diff against committed resource snapshots, and the diff is a CI gate — so a resource change without a migration fails the build rather than surfacing at deploy time.
questions.test: Check Ash-generated code is committed

questions.question: Can you tell what is happening in production?
questions.answer: Instrumentation is the `ash_enterprise_telemetry` package (`telemetry/`, on main): `AshEnterprise.Telemetry.setup/1` registers the Ash tracer, so every action, query and calculation becomes a span with no per-resource wiring, plus Phoenix, Ecto, Oban, outbound HTTP and GenAI spans, with correlation ids carried across them. The OTLP exporter is switched on by `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` in `config/runtime.exs`; with it unset nothing is exported, and a bounded in-memory trace ring serves the dev loop. ADR 0065 chose the receiving end, SigNoz for traces, logs and metrics and GlitchTip for errors, superseding ADR 0018, and `devenv/observability` runs both beside the application in development. Not here: this host does not enable error reporting to GlitchTip, and no deployment we operate runs the backends, collects the signals or alerts on them.

questions.question: How do enterprise customers bring their own identity provider?
questions.answer: One identity provider per deployment, over OpenID Connect (ADR 0071). The user resource declares an `oidc` strategy when the build sets `OIDC_BASE_URL`; the issuer, client and secret are read at runtime, and a build without them shows no provider button. A first sign-in links the provider's subject only to an existing user who is active, has confirmed the address here, and whose email the provider marks verified. An unknown address, an unverified email, an unconfirmed or deactivated user, a subject already linked to someone else and a second subject for one user are all refused, and no user is ever created. Each attempt is recorded at the `oidc` sign-in door without the email, and the provider's access and refresh tokens are not kept. The provider then owns the second factor, password policy and when a person leaves. Not built: SAML, a provider per organisation, and SCIM provisioning. Not yet running in a deployment we operate.
questions.test: a verified, confirmed, active user signs in, the identity is recorded, and the token lives the configured 8 hours

questions.question: How do accounts appear and disappear when someone joins or leaves?
questions.answer: Joining and leaving are in-app actions today, and a directory does not drive them. Joining: registration creates a user with a confirmation email, and the seeder provisions confirmed users. Leaving: the platform lifecycle's `deactivate` action turns a user inactive. A deactivated user with the right password cannot sign in, a bearer token issued earlier stops authenticating and is revoked (reactivating does not revive it), a session subject no longer resolves, a password reset finds nobody inactive, an API key follows its owner, and the user is no longer a member of the tenant, so it loses its actions and its rows. Role grants can carry `valid_until` and are gone at that instant. The deactivation is recorded in each organization the person belongs to, and the `offboarding` pack (`priv/packs/offboarding/`, installed as drafts) matches it: once a person publishes it with `publish_granted`, its steps run as the recipe runner acting for them, revoke any session still live, archive the leaver's API keys so a reactivation does not revive them, record what the leaver holds there (owned records, open tasks, running processes, recipes, role assignments), and open a review for another administrator. A person reactivated before the run is not touched, and under a revoked or lapsed grant the run records `no_authority` and changes nothing (`test/ash_enterprise/accounts/offboarding_test.exs`). Role assignments are not ended by the recipe, because ending one changes authority and no automation principal does that: while the account is inactive they cannot act, and the review lists them for a person to end. What is missing: no directory is wired in, since there is no SCIM endpoint and `ash_scim` is not a dependency, so departure still depends on someone here being told.
questions.test: a deactivated user with the right password does not

questions.question: What second factor is required, and how are sessions bounded?
questions.answer: Sessions are bounded at the token, the cookie and the socket; the second factor is the identity provider's. The session token lives 8 hours, set explicitly (`Accounts.TokenPolicy`, host-configurable, a malformed setting raises rather than defaulting), is stored server-side so it can be revoked, and is revoked on deactivation and on a password change. The browser session cookie's max age is the same lifetime, and a LiveView connected before the token expired stops at its expiry rather than acting on. Before each event an open LiveView also checks, as a new request would, that its token is still stored and unrevoked and its user can still sign in, so deactivation or a password change stops it at its next event. Five failed password sign-ins lock an identity for 15 minutes. No in-app strategy requires a second factor: with sign-in through the deployment's OIDC provider (q29) the second factor and step-up are the provider's, and this application does not require the provider to assert one.
questions.test: a live view connected before the token expired stops acting after it

questions.question: Who may act as someone else, and is that recorded differently from acting as yourself?
questions.answer: Acting as someone else is gated, recorded and expiring. The record's `created_on_behalf_by_id` names the operator while `created_by_id` names the customer, and every audit event carries `impersonator_id`. A break-glass session names the operator, the person acted as, a written reason of at least 10 characters, a named approver and an expiry (240 minutes at most, host-configurable). Opening one is a request; it is live only after the named approver approves it, a separate audited act by an active person who is neither the operator nor the subject. Opening and approving need a grant and a human actor, never a system actor or an impersonating one. The session ends at its expiry instant, when ended, or when the operator or subject is deactivated. Not built: telling the account owner when a session opens.
questions.test: a live session yields an actor attributed to the operator

questions.question: Can the audit log be altered after the fact?
questions.answer: Shipped. Two mechanisms with different jobs: a trigger refuses `UPDATE` and `DELETE` outright, and every event carries a SHA-256 chained to the previous one, so an operator privileged enough to drop the trigger still cannot make an edit look untouched. `mix ash_enterprise.audit.verify` walks the chains; the suite proves it by tampering.
questions.test: an altered row is found

questions.question: Can a customer see their own audit trail, and only theirs?
questions.answer: Shipped. The log is attribute-multitenant on an `organization_id` the chain trigger derives from stamped metadata, so a tenant-scoped read is filtered by the data layer rather than by a policy written specially for the audit log. Depth answers how much of a tenant you see; tenancy answers which tenant.
questions.test: a tenant does not see another tenant's events

questions.question: Can an auditor be handed a window of evidence without engineering help?
questions.answer: Shipped. `mix ash_enterprise.audit.export --from --to [--tenant]` writes CSV in chain order, including `sequence`, `previous_hash` and `hash` so the recipient can re-verify it rather than take it on trust. It reads through the ordinary action layer, so an export is exactly as wide as its requester's authorization.
questions.test: the export is scoped exactly as the reader is

questions.question: How long is evidence kept, and where does it live after ninety days?
questions.answer: Ninety days hot, then archived; never purged before four hundred days from when it was recorded (`AshEnterprise.Audit.Retention`, daily). Audit events and superseded evidence artifacts older than ninety days move to `audit_event_archive` and `evidence_artifact_archive`, tables in the same database. Each move copies the rows, compares the copy (count, every column, a SHA-256 digest over the hashes, and each artifact's content against its hash) and deletes the hot rows only when that holds; a failed comparison deletes nothing and is recorded. One tenant's chain that cannot be verified is recorded as a failed run and does not stop the others, and a backlog larger than one run may move is reported and drains over the following runs. The immutability trigger allows a delete only of a row past ninety days with an identical archived copy, and the archive's triggers refuse every update and any delete under four hundred days, counted for evidence from the later of its stated collection time and when it was recorded, so a back-dated artifact is not purged early. Purging is off unless configured, refused under 400, and the chain still verifies across hot, archived and purged rows. Not partitioned: ADR 0024's partitions were never created, so the archive is tables, not detached partitions. Partial because expiry has not yet run in a deployment we operate, so no verified archive run is recorded outside the tests, and the archive is only as durable as the deployment's backups (q48).
questions.test: a 399-day row is never purged

questions.question: Are role and permission changes attributable to a person?
questions.answer: Shipped. Role assignments are ordinary audited resources, so granting one produces an event naming the grantor, the grantee and the correlation id of the request — and the record itself now carries `created_by_id`, which nothing populated before.
questions.test: assigning a role records the grantor, the grantee and the request's correlation id

questions.question: Where are logs reviewed, and what raises an alarm on a declared audited event?
questions.answer: Alarms on declared audited events are raised in a tenant, and each leaves a record that a person reviewed it. The `security_alerts` pack (`priv/packs/security_alerts/`, installed as drafts), once a person publishes it, opens a review for an administrator other than the people involved when an Administrator or Platform Operator role is assigned, a break-glass session is approved, an API key is issued, a known person's sign-in is refused for the third time in a row, or a SigNoz alert labelled `security` arrives (a GlitchTip alert arrives as an error and never does). The reviewer's answer is the record that someone looked, and the event next to each alarm (another role, an unapproved session, a revoked key, two refusals, another alert category) opens nothing (`test/ash_enterprise/bpmn/alert_review_test.exs`). Inbound alerts come through a signed webhook (`POST /webhooks/alerts-signoz`, `/webhooks/alerts-glitchtip`): each key maps to one organization, and a replay or an unsigned, wrongly signed, stale or other-tenant call records nothing (`test/ash_enterprise_web/alert_webhook_test.exs`). SigNoz is the deployment's log review and alerting: every Ash action reaches it over OTLP as a span carrying the actor (ADR 0065), and the rules in `devenv/observability/security/alerts/` run on those spans across tenants, including refused sign-ins for addresses with no account. SigNoz is an observability platform, not a full SIEM: no detection-rule library, threat intelligence or cross-source correlation. Spans can be sampled and expire, so the tamper-evident audit log itself does not yet reach SigNoz (planned: committed audit events as OpenTelemetry log records). The rules notify nobody until a channel is set up, and neither tool signs a webhook, so their alerts reach the webhook only through a signing relay the owner supplies. Shipping to a customer's own SIEM is ADR 0025 (proposed). What is only logged: every other audited write (role revocations, privilege and posture changes, data changes, exports), refused sign-ins below the third, and every read, since reads are not audited. There is no review rota beyond these tasks, and the review proves that someone answered, not that the answer was right.
questions.test: when an Administrator is made, offered to neither the granter nor the grantee

questions.question: What crosses the tenant boundary, and to whom?
questions.answer: A design-time register of egress paths, generated into `docs/data-inventory.json` beside the inventory: one row per way data leaves the database (the provider proxy, guarded and judgment model calls, the assistant runtime, lineage events, account mail, trace export, the golden-record and audit exports, and every operation declared through `AshOperations`, read from its DSL). Each row names the class of recipient, the classes of data it can carry, and the gate that governs it, or says `none` with the gap in prose: the provider proxy and account mail have no tenant-level gate, and the guarded model path consults the deployment-wide in-zone flag but not the tenant's recorded opt-in. A test scans `lib/` for egress shapes and fails on a module that holds one and is in no row; it is a text scan with a known list of shapes, so a client library outside the list passes unseen. Not built: a list of a deployment's live sub-processors (the register names classes of recipient; the deployment owner records the actual vendors), a tenant-facing report, and an attestation of what a running deployment sent.
questions.test: a module in lib/ that calls an egress primitive (Req, ReqLLM, Swoosh delivery, use AshOperations, the lineage transport) and is not in the register fails

questions.question: What does an AI model see, and can a customer opt out?
questions.answer: Partial. Thesis 5 settles the authorization half: an agent is an actor with an actor's permissions, so a model reaches nothing its user could not. ADR 0042 settles disclosure for inference: an instrument inside the data's own zone is not a disclosure and is recorded in the judgment ledger, and a sub-processor is refused unless the tenant has recorded an opt-in on its organization, which is data and is audited like any update. Every unknown case is a refusal, and `REQUIRE_IN_ZONE_MODELS` refuses sub-processors for everyone. The residency policy test asserts these. A model call's record (`AshEnterprise.AI.ModelCall`) holds its provider, model and usage, never its content, and an agent run's journal keeps the turns, sealed under the subject's erasure key (ADR 0056). ADR 0026 is still proposed, and there is no tenant-facing report of what a vendor saw.

questions.question: How do other systems find out that something happened here?
questions.answer: Open. Events land in the audit log and go nowhere else. There is no outbound webhook, no subscription, and no delivery guarantee for anyone who needs to react to a change rather than poll for it.

questions.question: How does a customer get fifty thousand rows in, or out?
questions.answer: Open. JSON:API and GraphQL paginate, and neither is a bulk path. Import exists only as a Meltano-shaped plan; export exists only for the audit log.

questions.question: Can a deploy happen without downtime, and can a migration be reversed?
questions.answer: Partial. Every generated migration has a `down`, and `ash_strangler`'s four-phase cutover is built precisely so a legacy migration can be reversed at any phase. What is untested is the app's own rolling deploy: nothing proves an old and a new node can serve the same schema at once, which is the property zero-downtime actually needs.

questions.question: Does it still work for a customer with fifty thousand of something?
questions.answer: Built and measured on CI; not yet running in a deployment we operate, so the status waits for that. Every list read on a platform resource names a page size: a transformer gives each read that is not a get or a manual read a `default_limit` of 50 and a `max_page_size` of 250, so a page asked for without a limit gets 50 rows and no request gets more than 250, while an internal read that asks for no page still returns a list. The JSON:API index and the GraphQL list on business units, teams and positions serve a `:list` read whose paging is required, so a request that names no page gets 50 rows and a next link, never the table; a test walks every index route, list query and AI read tool and fails on one that could return a table. The `scale` CI job seeds 50,000 audited teams in one tenant: an unpaged JSON:API index, its next page and a GraphQL list each issue the same 12 queries at 1,000 rows and at 50,000 (at 50,000 rows the index and its next page took 83 ms each and the list 59 ms on a CI runner, against ceilings of three times the first CI measurement), and a business-unit-depth role's page is one query, on teams (25 ms). Seeding the 50,000 took 92 s. The numbers are the template's own seeded fixture on CI hardware, not any deployment's. Not measured at that size: writes, exports, the A2UI surfaces, the AI lookups that read a window before keeping their first rows, and every resource other than teams.
questions.test: every JSON:API index, GraphQL list and AshAi read tool pages by default

questions.question: Can a customer change how it behaves without a deploy?
questions.answer: Partial, and less partial than it was. A tenant can fork a process or a decision, edit it in the browser and publish it as its own version, with no binding row meaning 'follow the platform baseline' -- so changing behaviour is data, and reverting is deleting a row. Drift from a newer baseline is reported, never merged. What is still a deploy: adding an attribute is a resource change and a migration, and a tenant can try a draft or published decision against sample inputs before publishing it (the Try it panel at `/app/decisions/:key/try`, which records nothing and is covered in `test/ash_enterprise_web/live/decisions/try_live_test.exs`).

questions.question: Which named controls does any of this actually satisfy?
questions.answer: Partial. `docs/COMPLIANCE.md` maps 7 SOC 2 criteria, 4 ISO 27001 controls and 4 GDPR articles to the questions above and through them to the proof of each, generated from the same ledger so it cannot drift. `docs/controls.json` also carries an ownership row for each of the 61 SOC 2 criteria: a class, an owner role, and the evidence producer, operating process and test wherever one exists. 31 rows have nothing missing; 30 still lack a process, a test or a producer, and CI lists every missing piece (`mix ash_compliance.controls.check --report`) while a test refuses a reference that does not resolve. The 19 operator process templates `ash_compliance` ships each have one row in the `soc2` pack's map (`priv/packs/soc2/`): eight are recipes that open a human-only review (seven on a schedule, one on an inbound alert), four reuse a recipe or process the application already has, and seven carry the reason no audited event can start them; a test refuses a template with no row or two, an empty row or a recipe nothing uses. That closed 30 of the 101 missing pieces (71 remain). The pack installs as drafts and nothing runs until a person publishes it. A row says who owns a criterion, not that it operates; evidence is recorded only where a producer exists (the daily chain verification records CC4.1 and CC7.2), and every other criterion reads as unknown. An auditor can be handed the result: `mix ash_enterprise.audit.export --tenant --as --from --to --out` writes one tenant's audit package for a period, behind its own privilege (`read` on `AshEnterprise.Audit.Package`, global only): the criteria in scope with each one's control-file row, the evidence collected with each criterion's freshness at the period's end, the open findings, the review tasks and their outcomes, and the audit chain's verification, as plain JSON and as OSCAL 1.2.3 assessment results built by `ash_compliance`, whose suite validates them against NIST's published schema. It never reports a criterion as satisfied: unknown evidence is a not-satisfied finding, and the rest are observations. The map covers technical prerequisites only; certification also needs policy, process and an auditor, and the document says so first rather than last.

questions.question: What is promised about uptime, and what happens when it is missed?
questions.answer: Open: the template now says how uptime is expressed and measured, and the promise is still the owner's. `GET /health` answers without a sign-in and carries no data: 200 when the database and the job runner answer, 503 otherwise, the status, the version and each check (`test/ash_enterprise_web/health_test.exs`). A default objective is written down as SigNoz rules and a dashboard (`devenv/observability/slo/`): 99.5% of `/health` probes answered over 30 days, alerted on a fast and a slow error-budget burn and on no probe answered for 10 minutes, and p95 Ash action latency under 500 ms. Those numbers are unmeasured defaults, since nothing has run against them for 30 days. A missed objective is an alert, and an alert that reaches the application opens an incident (q49). What is the owner's: the prober that calls `/health`, the number actually promised to customers, a status page, and what a missed month costs. The SLI is measured where the application answers, so a node that answers nothing shows only as missing probes.
questions.test: a failing check answers 503, names the check and says nothing else

questions.question: How quickly can you come back from losing the database?
questions.answer: A backup and restore drill exists and CI runs it on every push to main and to `ci/**` branches, and on every pull request: `scripts/backup-restore-drill` dumps the database with `pg_dump -Fc` from one snapshot, restores it into a fresh database, and checks the copy (every table's row count against the snapshot, every audit chain verified on the copy), reporting the dump's size, SHA-256 and how long the dump and restore took; a tampered chain or a missing row fails it. The `backup-restore-drill` CI job runs it against a seeded database on the service Postgres, and `docs/runbooks/backup-and-restore.md` is the procedure. Partial because it is measured at seed scale only and the drill is a script, not a named test. Nothing here configures where backups are stored, how often they run, point-in-time recovery or replication, and no RPO or RTO is committed to: those come from running the drill on a deployment's own data.

questions.question: When something breaks at three in the morning, what happens?
questions.answer: Partial: what happens is written down and built up to a task, and the rest is the owner's (`docs/runbooks/incident-response.md`). A SigNoz or GlitchTip alert that reaches the inbound alert webhook (q38) is recorded in the key's organization as an `alert.firing` occurrence and opens an incident there; a duplicate for the same rule joins the open incident instead of opening a second, and a resolved alert closes it. Once a person publishes the `incident_triage` pack (`priv/packs/incident_triage/`, installed as drafts, human tasks only), opening an incident gives the tenant's starter On-call role one triage task on the task list, which a person resolves or escalates to an administrator; a person not on call neither sees nor takes it, another tenant's alert opens nothing, and every step is in the audit chain (`test/ash_enterprise/bpmn/incident_triage_pack_test.exs`, and end to end through the webhook in `test/ash_enterprise_web/incident_webhook_test.exs`). Still missing: neither tool signs a webhook, so a relay that holds the key is the owner's; the task list wakes nobody; and the rota, a pager and what the customer is told are the owner's.
questions.test: a duplicate alert joins the open incident instead of opening a second

questions.question: What is in the build, and can you prove nothing else is?
questions.answer: Partial. CI runs `mix hex.audit` for retired packages and `mix sobelow` for web vulnerabilities on every push, `mix.lock` pins everything transitively, the Dockerfile pins Elixir, OTP and the base image, and a test fails when a git dependency or an override is missing from `docs/BLEEDING-EDGE.md`. CI has no schedule, so a vulnerability published after the last push is not seen, and no dependency update service is configured. There is no SBOM, no signed build and no provenance attestation, so the dependency set is checked but not attested.

questions.question: Can you show a control operated continuously for twelve months?
questions.answer: Partial. This is the question the rest of the section is really asking. What exists: an unbroken, verifiable hash chain covering every write, exportable per tenant for any window, and an ownership row for each SOC 2 criterion in `docs/controls.json`. Now scheduled: every chain, hot and archived, is verified daily and the result stored as an evidence artifact for CC4.1 and CC7.2, findings included (`AshEnterprise.Audit.ChainVerifyWorker`), and `ash_compliance`'s freshness sweep runs hourly for every organization, so a daily control whose last result is older than a day becomes an open `:unknown` finding, and is resolved when fresh evidence arrives. Retention keeps the window: ninety days hot, nothing purged before four hundred (q36). The audit package (`mix ash_enterprise.audit.export`, q46) hands an auditor any period of it for one tenant: how many daily verifications were recorded, every artifact with its hash re-checked, each criterion's freshness at the period's end, and the chain verified whole, hot and archived; a chain that does not verify is reported as broken, in the JSON and as an OSCAL finding, never passed over. Still missing: twelve months of it actually running, most criteria having no producer recording evidence at all (they read as unknown), and any evidence that anyone reviewed the log (q38).
questions.test: a stale verification produces its overdue finding

questions.question: How are business rules expressed, versioned and changed without a deploy?
questions.answer: As DMN, in `ash_decisions`. A decision is a DMN document -- the single artifact, with no second copy of the rules in a table to drift from it -- versioned and immutable on publish, edited in dmn-js, and evaluated either by a business rule task inside a process or by trigger routing deciding which process to start. The engine is adopted rather than written and measured at 97.68% of the official DMN TCK. `OUTPUT ORDER` and `RULE ORDER` are refused at compile time because both make document order semantically significant, which is the same order-dependence the authorization model rejects. Publishing runs a verifier over every decision table: overlapping rules under `UNIQUE` or `ANY`, gaps in the input space and rules that can never fire are proved, an error-severity finding blocks the publish, and whatever the verifier cannot decide is recorded as an open obligation rather than reported clean. Every evaluation records which version decided, what it saw and which rules fired. An author can run any readable version against sample inputs before publishing, on the Try it panel at `/app/decisions/:key/try`: typed inputs, the answer, the rules that matched and the hit policy, with invalid input refused and no `Evaluation` written (`test/ash_enterprise_web/live/decisions/try_live_test.exs`; the version resolver is covered in `test/ash_enterprise/process/decision_resolver_test.exs`). What is missing is the panel inside the dmn-js editor itself, a way to try a platform baseline without customising it, and sample inputs saved with the draft.
questions.test: trying writes no Evaluation

questions.question: Can a UI built on the new model be driven by a database the old application still owns?
questions.answer: Yes, and it is demonstrated rather than asserted: `INSERT INTO legacy.users` in `psql` reaches a surface generated from `AshEnterprise.Accounts.ProjectedUser` -- an Ash-owned table with real columns -- without a reload and without anything in that surface knowing a legacy database exists. The chain is an `AFTER` trigger, `pg_notify` on commit, a durable ledger row written in the legacy transaction, a drain worker that upserts through an ordinary Ash action, and `Ash.Notifier.PubSub`. What it costs: the projection is eventually consistent, and `projected_at` is a column so the lag is on screen rather than hidden. A row that fails to project is retried by the drain (ten attempts, a five-minute sweep behind it), and a nightly reconcile compares the legacy view with the projected table, repairs disagreeing key ranges as the drain ingests a row (the same projection entry point and the KYC compliance events, in one transaction) and reports counts and key ranges; a projected row whose legacy row was hard-deleted is reported and never deleted. What is left: drift is telemetry only (no stored run record, no finding), and the scope is one entity on a same-instance schema with no cutover.

questions.question: How does production data reach an environment where the rules that protect it do not run?
questions.answer: A dump pipeline, not the action layer: greenmask transforms a pg_dump in flight, and its config is generated from the resource declarations by a proposed first-party extension — a `sensitive?` attribute with no declared transform fails generation rather than passing through, and referential continuity comes from greenmask's hash engine with an env-injected salt. The extension is built and public (`lukegalea/ash_greenmask`); this app has not adopted it yet.

items.title: Legacy migration, process modelling and decisions as platform extensions
items.choice: ash_strangler + ash_bpmn + ash_decisions, first-party
items.effort: Three packages at 0.1.0 under MIT with substantial suites -- 341 tests for the strangler, 198 for BPMN, 101 plus a 3,495-assertion conformance corpus for decisions. The composition is what was outstanding and is now done: all three are dependencies, their resources sit on this application's base resource, a process runs here end to end, and the legacy estate is both read live through a view and projected into a table this application owns.
items.bar: Yes for both, now. `ash_strangler` by construction — its output is read through the ordinary action layer. `ash_bpmn` because a work item on `AshEnterprise.Platform.Resource` inherits this policy set, with one ordering rule: Ash's bypasses skip only the policies declared after them, so the engine's bypass has to sit at the top of `AshEnterprise.Security.Policies` or the engine acts as a `SystemActor` this set already admits.
items.answer: All three are dependencies of this application and their resources are this application's own: a legacy table is mapped and read here, and the process, decision and trigger tables inherit `AshEnterprise.Platform.Resource` -- so an instance is an ordinary owned, tenant-scoped, audited record and the engines' authority is two declared policy bypasses rather than an option at a call site. Demonstrated rather than asserted: an `AccessRequest` submission is one audited write, a trigger matches it, a FEEL guard filters it, a DMN decision routes it, and four seeded requests drive all three branches of the gateway. What is not here is a FEEL editor, and decision evaluation from the editor.

items.title: Data ingestion
items.choice: Meltano (MIT); Airbyte as the fallback
items.effort: Landed: an Oban wrapper job runs a Meltano/Singer tap, parses its output and lands raw rows as `SourceObject` records through an Ash action — an operator-only, untenanted landing zone sealed per erasure scope (ADR 0024), with host-declared projections promoting into canonical resources and lineage Job events from the wrapper. Gmail, Calendar and Slack arrive through the Nango proxy (ADR 0011) into the same landing zone. ADR 0010's implementation note records the deviation from its staging-schema boundary. Zones admission (ADR 0042) gates Gmail and Slack projection into the canonical store on each linked account's operator-set tags, and what it admits is owner-only. Pending: `mix meltano.gen.resource`, a committed `meltano.yml` for non-dev pipelines, append-only landing and a stream-aware identity, Zones admission on the raw land path itself.
items.bar: No, by refusal: Meltano is kept outside the boundary where authorization applies, so there is no second model to synchronize. Raw rows land as platform resources (tenant-scoped, policy-gated on read); the residual is that landing writes run system-side with authorize?: false, and a pipeline landing two tenants into one table is a defect the platform cannot detect.

items.title: Integration hub — avoiding M×N
items.choice: Nango for the provider edge only
items.effort: Built for Google Calendar, Gmail and Slack (2026-10-12): provider operations are declared and generated as Ash actions that call Nango's proxy (`AshEnterprise.Integration.Nango`), an Oban cron scheduler runs one sync step per linked account, and everything a sync lands is sealed under that account's erasure scope (ADR 0024). Not built: webhooks (everything polls), a production Nango deployment, and promoting the extension into its own package.
items.bar: Yes, with one load-bearing rule: the Nango connection id is never an action argument — it is resolved inside the action from the actor's own linked account (ADR 0011, deviation 1). Otherwise the policy engine authorizes the operation while the caller picks whose credentials to spend. The residual is stated, not wrapped away: anyone holding the Nango secret key bypasses every policy.

items.title: Lineage and provenance
items.choice: OpenLineage + Marquez
items.effort: Emitter shipped as ash_open_lineage (github.com/lukegalea/ash_open_lineage): Spark `lineage` extension + notifier on the platform base resource, spec 2-0-2 fixture conformance, red-green leak test, live verification against a local Marquez (tap runs input→output, failing taps emit FAIL). Deviations from this entry's wording, recorded: runIds are per-(correlation, job) — sha256(correlation/namespace/job) — because one correlation spans many jobs and a shared runId collapses them in consumers; the raw correlation id rides the producer facet so the audit↔lineage lookup still holds. Known gaps: ingestion Job events can be lost on VM shutdown (async transport), no tap→land parent link yet, and the ingestion job's dataset names do not yet join the notifier's table datasets.
items.bar: Marquez has no authorization model at all — which forces two rules: deploy it like `clarity`, behind the same boundary, and never put a value, actor or tenant into a facet. No verifier enforces the second.

items.title: Approvals and maker-checker
items.choice: ash_bpmn — no external engine
items.effort: Built and tested in the package, including duplicate refusal via a partial unique index and timer cancellation, and now running here: a manager approval and an executive approval are both reachable from the seeded demo and both appear on `/app/tasks` behind the actor's principal ids. Remaining, and the reason this is not shipped: no test asserts the *negative* -- that a user without the privilege cannot decide a task -- which is this file's own bar.
items.bar: The decisive argument against Camunda or Flowable — an external engine is a second authorization and data model to keep in sync, and it would express maker-checker as a deny rule, which this repository forbids.
items.answer: `ash_bpmn` adopted, with its work item on the platform base resource and the engine's authority declared as the first bypass in the base's policy set rather than as an option at a call site. Maker-checker is applied by subtraction at candidate resolution, never as a `forbid_if`. Decisions a process routes on are `ash_decisions`. A process runs here and people can complete its tasks; what is still missing is the test that would fail if the wrong person could.

items.title: Business rules and decision tables
items.choice: ash_decisions — DMN, engine adopted not written
items.effort: A first-party package over `boxic_dmn`/`boxic_feel`: versioned immutable definitions, tenancy, the authorization bypass, the evaluation log, the dmn-js editor, and an independent run of the official DMN TCK as the gate. 101 tests plus 3,495 corpus assertions.
items.bar: The measurement, not the preference. Writing a conforming FEEL implementation is a 60–90 person-day project; an independent TCK run put the existing engine at 97.68% before any work of ours, so it was adopted. What makes a 0.x package by one author defensible is that it sits behind a single adapter module and the conformance suite is ours — replacing it is measurable rather than speculative.
items.answer: DMN, as its own first-party package. The DMN document is the single artifact — no second copy of the rules in a table — versioned per tenant, evaluated by a business rule task or by trigger routing, and edited in dmn-js. **97.68% of the official DMN TCK** (3,414 of 3,495 asserted result nodes; level 2 96.83%, level 3 97.71%), with each remaining failure listed against a measured node count so the gate fails if it moves in either direction. Publish-time verification proves overlaps, gaps and rules that can never fire, and blocks a publish on an error-severity finding; each evaluation records which rules fired. Not shipped: a way to evaluate a decision against sample inputs from the editor.

items.title: Rules and compliance as data
items.choice: ash_rules (rule IR + swappable evaluators) and ash_compliance (governed layering compiled to immutable bundles, findings projected from events)
items.effort: The KYC vertical slice is live in the reference app: catalogs, profiles, waivers and tenant policy sets compile through the fixed precedence into content-hashed bundles; the strangler ledger feeds the projector; findings and append-only evaluations answer both 'now' and 'why'. Remaining: OSCAL component-definitions, evidence-of-review, and the generated controls.json/COMPLIANCE.md mapping (the `controls` row).
items.bar: Replay determinism: the same events under the same bundle produce byte-identical findings and evaluations, asserted by the test suite. A demo that could not replay would not be a compliance engine.

items.title: Data catalog and governance
items.choice: OpenMetadata (DataHub is the closer call it looks)
items.effort: A push step alongside `mix ash.codegen`, writing each resource's declared metadata over the REST API as a bot. Two stateful services, not one: OpenMetadata requires Elasticsearch or OpenSearch as well as Postgres.
items.bar: The least comfortable answer of the set. OpenMetadata's RBAC has Allow/Deny rules where deny wins — the exact inverse of a pure union — so no attempt is made to mirror roles into it, and the catalogue can therefore never face tenants.

items.title: Reporting and embedded analytics
items.choice: Apache Superset over Metabase
items.effort: Tenant- and role-scoped views generated from the existing actor context, so Superset's own RLS config is a formality.
items.bar: The deciding factor. Metabase paywalls row-level security even when self-hosted, which would put this project's central thesis behind a paywall.

items.title: API versioning and deprecation
items.choice: ash_api_versioning
items.effort: A new extension. No new database objects — that property is what makes it categorically cheaper than the strangler, and losing it makes it pointless.
items.bar: Not applicable — this is ours, and it wraps the action layer rather than bypassing it.

items.title: Feature flags and progressive delivery
items.choice: Tenant flag rows resolved into ActorContext (FunWithFlags and Unleash not adopted)
items.effort: Built: a declared catalogue, an audited tenant-scoped Flag resource targeting people, teams, business-unit subtrees and a stable percentage, resolved once per request into ActorContext, a deployment kill switch (FLAGS_OFF), and a mix task. Remaining: the first feature gated behind a flag in a deployment we operate, and a management screen.
items.bar: A flag check never queries and a flag is never authorization. FunWithFlags (ADR 0016, superseded) would have kept flags in a table outside the platform resource, so a flip would not be audited and a flag would not be a tenant's; Unleash adds a second security model and its community Elixir SDK silently ignores segments.

items.title: Observability backend
items.choice: SigNoz and GlitchTip
items.effort: Instrumentation is built (`ash_enterprise_telemetry`) and the backends run in the development environment (`devenv/observability`). What remains is running them in a deployment we operate, reading what they collect, and alerting on it. ADR 0018 proposed Grafana LGTM and is superseded.
items.bar: Not applicable — telemetry is not an authorization surface.

items.title: Master data and entity resolution
items.choice: In-Ash resolution over CDM resources
items.effort: In-Ash resolution is built and green: mappings-as-data with fail-closed validation and draft-only AI proposals, temporal landing, deterministic+fuzzy matching banded by a DMN table, a steward queue with person-gated verdicts on a BPMN baseline, survivorship merge/unmerge with recorded provenance, SourceIdentity XREF, deterministic projection replay, quality rules + projector with a scheduled sweep into stewardship tasks, egress export behind a zone disclosure gate, and the UI flow from ImportLive (CSV upload, mapping, run) to the A2UI steward queue (MdmStewardUI at /app/mdm, which lists only candidates whose golden the reader may read), the import-batch board and the golden-records surface. Named limitations: findings reach stewardship by explicit start + cron sweep, not the audit-event BPMN subscription (documented non-viable); matching is deterministic + fuzzy only (no probabilistic linkage); egress export is a code interface with no UI; no bulk re-match tooling.
items.bar: A golden record inside the platform inherits ownership, audit and policy. Two consequences fall out that an external hub hides: candidate generation must run as a system actor, so the review queue can leak the existence of duplicates; and a merge can revoke a user's access without revoking any grant, because grants are per-record and the record moved. AtroCore is GPL-3.0, not the MIT its own marketing claims; Pimcore left open source entirely in 2025.

items.title: Audit retention, partitioning and erasure
items.choice: Time-partitioned hot/cold split; erasure by crypto-shredding
items.effort: Erasure is built: per-scope data keys wrapped under a configured master key, one key per scope enforced by constraint, content sealed into `ash_cloak` columns under its scope's key, and a policy-gated, audited `shred_scope` that leaves the audit chain verifying (`AshEnterprise.Erasure`, `docs/runbooks/crypto-shredding.md`). Retention by age is built without partitions: ninety days hot, then a verified move to archive tables in the same database, nothing purged before four hundred days, and the chain still verifies (q36). Monthly partitions on `audit_events` detached to cheaper storage are still planned.
items.bar: No external tool. Retention is a property of the log, and the log is the thing this platform's audit story rests on — handing it to something outside the boundary would put the evidence chain outside it too.

items.title: Control mapping and evidence
items.choice: Generated from the ledger; SOC 2, ISO 27001, GDPR
items.effort: `docs/controls.json` maps control ids to ledger questions and their proofs, rendered into `docs/COMPLIANCE.md` and the site by the same task that renders the roadmap. It also holds an ownership row per SOC 2 criterion, checked in CI by `ash_compliance` and a test; 46 of 61 rows still name a missing process, test or producer. Remaining: those pieces, an evidence producer that records dated artifacts, the evidence-of-review half (which needs the SIEM item), and per-control screenshots an auditor can be handed.
items.bar: The map claims technical prerequisites and says so in its first paragraph. Claiming more would make the honesty mechanism the rest of this repository is built on worthless.

items.title: Enterprise identity: SAML, OIDC and SCIM
items.choice: Federate to the enterprise IdP over OIDC today; SAML and SCIM as planned strategies on the same seam
items.effort: OIDC with one provider per deployment is built through the library's strategy (ADR 0071), with no provisioning: a first sign-in links only to a confirmed account whose email the provider verifies. SAML needs a new strategy and an XML signature story. SCIM is the larger piece and the more interesting one here: provisioning maps onto ordinary create and lifecycle actions, so it is an endpoint over existing actions rather than a parallel user store.
items.bar: Yes. An identity provider authenticates; it never authorizes. Group-to-role mapping stays here as `(role, privilege, depth)` rows, which is the difference between an IdP telling us who you are and an IdP telling us what you may do.

items.title: Break-glass and impersonation control
items.choice: In-Ash: a session resource with a stated reason
items.effort: Built: attribution on records and events, and a session resource carrying who, whom, why, the approver and the expiry, gated by a privilege and by a second person's approval. Remaining: a notification to the account owner, which is the control customers actually ask for.
items.bar: No external tool. Who may act as whom is an authorization question, and this platform already has exactly one place authorization is expressed.

items.title: Log shipping, review and alerting
items.choice: Structured export to the customer's SIEM; SigNoz for ours (ADR 0065)
items.effort: A notifier streaming audit events as structured JSON to a customer-configured sink, per tenant, with the chain hashes intact so the copy is verifiable against the original. Alerting rules follow the same ledger the control map does.
items.bar: Partial by design: a SIEM cannot consume ActorContext, so the boundary is that it receives only what one tenant is entitled to and never a cross-tenant stream.

items.title: SLOs, disaster recovery and incident response
items.choice: Committed RPO/RTO with a tested restore; error budgets
items.effort: A restore drill in CI against a real dump is the load-bearing piece — an untested backup is a belief. SLOs and error budgets sit on the telemetry that already exists; the status page and rota are process rather than code, and are named as such.
items.bar: Not applicable in the usual sense, and worth saying so: these are operational commitments, not tools with authorization models. The bar they have to clear is that they are tested rather than asserted.

items.title: Outbound events and subscriptions
items.choice: An Ash notifier over the existing event log
items.effort: The audit log already contains every change with an actor and a tenant. A subscription is a filtered, tenant-scoped view of it with delivery and retry — which is Oban's job, not a new event system's.
items.bar: Yes, and unusually cleanly: a subscription is a read, so it is filtered by the same policies as any other read. A customer cannot subscribe to what they cannot see.

items.title: Bulk import and export
items.choice: Ash bulk actions over a staged upload
items.effort: `Ash.bulk_create` and `Ash.bulk_update` already exist and are authorized per record. The work is the staging surface, the error report a user can act on, and streaming exports that do not load a tenant into memory — the audit export is the pattern.
items.bar: Yes. Bulk is the same actions in a loop, so ownership, tenancy and audit apply per row rather than being skipped for speed.

items.title: Data inventory, classification and sub-processors
items.choice: Derived from resource metadata, not maintained by hand
items.effort: Every resource already declares its CDM provenance, ownership type and tenancy scope. Classification is one more declaration, and the inventory is then generated — the same argument as the control map, and the same reason it will still be true in a year.
items.bar: Overlaps the catalog item deliberately: this is the compliance artefact, that is the discovery tool, and both should read from the same declarations.

items.title: SBOM and build provenance
items.choice: CycloneDX SBOM; attested builds
items.effort: An SBOM generated in CI and attached to each release, plus provenance attestation for the container. Small, mechanical, and asked about on every enterprise security questionnaire.
items.bar: Not applicable — nothing here touches the authorization model. It is on the list because it is asked for, and off priority 1 because nothing depends on it.

items.title: Zero-downtime deploys and reversible migrations
items.choice: Expand/contract, proven by a two-version test
items.effort: Every migration already has a `down`. What is missing is a test that an old and a new node can serve the same schema simultaneously, which is what zero-downtime actually requires and what `down` alone does not give.
items.bar: Not applicable. Named because 'reversible migrations' is on every enterprise checklist and this repository can currently only claim half of it.

items.title: Performance at enterprise data volumes
items.choice: A seeded large tenant and a query budget
items.effort: Seed a tenant with fifty thousand of the widest resource, then assert query counts and response times in CI. The interesting result is not the number; it is which of the inherited policies turn out to cost something at that size.
items.bar: Not applicable, but load-bearing for thesis 3: an authorization model that is elegant and slow is not a model anyone keeps.

items.title: AI governance: what leaves the tenant boundary
items.choice: Prompt/response logging as audit events; per-tenant opt-out
items.effort: Thesis 5 already did the hard part — an agent is an actor, so a model reaches nothing its user could not, and there is no agent-specific authorization path to secure. What is left is disclosure: log prompt and response as audit events under the same tenant and correlation id as the action they produced, record which model and vendor saw them, and let a tenant switch the whole thing off.
items.bar: Yes, and it is the clearest case in the set. An LLM provider is a service behind a network boundary that cannot consume ActorContext, so the rule from thesis 6 applies literally: it receives only what one actor was already entitled to, and removing it degrades a feature rather than breaking the app.

items.title: Pseudoanonymization of production data
items.choice: ash_greenmask — config generated from the resource declarations (greenmask, Apache-2.0, adopted not written). The package is built and public at lukegalea/ash_greenmask; this app has not adopted it yet
items.effort: A first-party extension in the ash_api_versioning shape: a `greenmask` block on the resource is the single declaration of what may leave production and how, `mix ash_greenmask.gen.config` emits greenmask's YAML from it plus what the model already knows (`sensitive?`, types, the ash_postgres table mapping), and CI gates both the drift between declarations and config and greenmask's own `validate --strict`. No database objects, nothing running in the application itself.
items.bar: Cleanly, by construction: greenmask is handed a thin generated declaration and holds no authorization model — it never serves a query. The control that stands in for ActorContext is the pipeline itself, the only door production bytes leave through, transformed before anything person-like sees them. The residuals are stated rather than wrapped away: the salt is load-bearing key material, hashed keys are not guaranteed unique, and what the config does not name passes through — which is why generation is refuse-by-default over `sensitive?`.
